svg.aria-label: Diagram: the Google Cloud load balancing decision tree; the first question is traffic type, where HTTP or HTTPS selects an Application Load Balancer, TCP with optional SSL offload selects a proxy Network Load Balancer, and preserving client source addresses or carrying UDP, ESP and ICMP selects a passthrough Network Load Balancer; the second question is external versus internal, and only external load balancers are available as global, so internal deployments spanning regions use a cross-region load balancer reached by a regional internal address from a subnet rather than a single anycast address, while regional internal load balancers accept only same-region clients until global access is enabled on the forwarding rule; the third question is proxy versus passthrough, where proxies terminate client connections on Google Front Ends or Envoy and send to backends from their own addresses, breaking authentication that tracks the first connection's source address, and passthrough leaves packet headers unchanged with responses returning directly to clients as direct server return; scope is also a compliance decision because global load balancers terminate TLS in globally distributed locations while regional ones guarantee termination in their own region, and resilience depends on backend redundancy as much as on load balancer scope; Envoy-based load balancers require a proxy-only subnet of at least 64 addresses with a /23 and its 512 addresses recommended, allocated at the VPC level and shared by every Envoy load balancer in that region, with only one active subnet per purpose per VPC and region; and two traps remain, that the global external Application Load Balancer and global external proxy Network Load Balancer exist only in Premium Tier, and that EXTERNAL_MANAGED backend services attach to EXTERNAL forwarding rules but not the reverse
svg.title: The load balancing decision tree: traffic type, then scope, then proxy or passthrough
svg.text: Three questions decide which of them you may use. Feature comparison comes after,
and only among the survivors.
QUESTION 1 — traffic type. “You must FIRST determine the traffic type.”
HTTP / HTTPS → APPLICATION LOAD BALANCER. “A flexible feature set for your applications.”
TCP, optional SSL offload → PROXY NETWORK LOAD BALANCER.
Need the CLIENT SOURCE IP, or UDP / ESP / ICMP → PASSTHROUGH NETWORK LOAD BALANCER.
Protocol breadth is where they differ most: internal passthrough carries 8 protocols including
SCTP and AH; external passthrough carries 6. Nothing else carries anything but TCP or HTTP(S).
QUESTION 2 — external or internal, and the asymmetry inside it
“ONLY EXTERNAL load balancers are available as GLOBAL load balancers.” There is no global
internal load balancer. For multi-region internal backends you use CROSS-REGION.
And cross-region is not global wearing a different name:
GLOBAL → a single ANYCAST address, with IPv6 termination at the load balancer.
CROSS-REGION → a REGIONAL INTERNAL address, from a subnet in the VPC network.
Regional internal accepts SAME-REGION clients only — until you enable GLOBAL ACCESS on the
forwarding rule. A one-flag difference that is easy to miss and easy to blame on routing.
QUESTION 3 — proxy or passthrough, and what each does to the packet
PROXY terminates the client connection on a GOOGLE FRONT END or an ENVOY proxy, then opens a
new connection to the backend. All Application LBs and all proxy Network LBs work this way.
PASSTHROUGH leaves source, destination and port UNCHANGED. Replies go straight back to the
client, not through the load balancer — DIRECT SERVER RETURN.
THE TRAP: proxies reach backends “from DIFFERENT GFE or Envoy IP addresses”. Authentication
that remembers which address opened the FIRST connection breaks. Google’s own advice is to
use IDENTITY-AWARE PROXY instead — or choose passthrough, which keeps the client address.
Scope is a compliance decision before it is a latency one
GLOBAL terminates TLS “in locations that are distributed globally” — good for latency, and a
problem if a regulator asks where the handshake happened.
REGIONAL “GUARANTEE that you terminate TLS ONLY in the region” where it is deployed. If you
need geographic control over TLS termination, this is the answer — not a feature flag.
Resilience: global survives a region; cross-region spans several; regional spans zones only, and
“an outage in a given region affects the regional load balancers in that region”.
The prerequisite nobody chose: the proxy-only subnet
Every ENVOY-based load balancer needs one. “Reserved exclusively for Envoy proxies … can’t be
used for any other purposes.” At least 64 addresses, so /26 or shorter; /23 (512) recommended.
“Proxies are allocated at the VPC LEVEL, not the load balancer level.” Every Envoy load balancer
in that region and network SHARES the subnet — so sizing it is a platform decision, not a
per-application one, and one team can exhaust another team’s proxies.
Only ONE active subnet per purpose per VPC per region: REGIONAL_MANAGED_PROXY for regional LBs
and Secure Web Proxy; GLOBAL_MANAGED_PROXY for the cross-region pair.
Two constraints that are not in the decision tree but will decide for you anyway:
• TIER — the global external Application LB and global external proxy NLB are PREMIUM TIER ONLY.
• SCHEME — EXTERNAL_MANAGED backends attach to EXTERNAL rules. The reverse is NOT allowed.
